body_md:
\label{example1}
Consider the graph $B_4(2,3,1,2)$  with vertex set $\{v_1,\ldots,v_8\}$. We order the vertices as
\[
v_1,v_2 \in K_2,\quad
v_3,v_4,v_5 \in K_3,\quad
v_6 \in K_1,\quad
v_7,v_8 \in K_2,
\]
as illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:graph-clouds}. In this case, $t=4$ and $(n_1,n_2,n_3,n_4) = (2,3,1,2)$.
Therefore, the matrix $M$ by  Theorem~\ref{thm:char_polynomial} is
\[
M =
\begin{bmatrix}
n_1-1 & n_2    & 0      & 0\\
n_1   & n_2-1  & 0      & n_4\\
0     & 0      & n_3-1  & n_4\\
0     & n_2    & n_3    & n_4-1
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 3 & 0 & 0\\
2 & 2 & 0 & 2\\
0 & 0 & 0 & 2\\
0 & 3 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

The eigenvalues of $M$ are
\[
\lambda_1 \approx 5.0899,\quad
\lambda_2 \approx 1.6266,\quad
\lambda_3 \approx -2.2956,\quad
\lambda_4 \approx -0.4209.
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:char_polynomial}, the spectrum of 
$B_4(2,3,1,2)$ is
$\{\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3,\lambda_4,-1,-1,-1,-1\}$.

label: eq:14
title: Proof
body_md:
Again we have
\begin{align}
    \operatorname{tr}(M^2)=\sum_{i,k} m_{ik}m_{ki}
&=\sum_{i=1}^{t}(n_i-1)^2 \;+\; \sum_{i\ne j} a_{ij}a_{ji}\,n_in_j \notag \\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{2s+1}(n_i-1)^2 \;+\; 2\sum_{1\le i<j\le 2s+1}\!\! a_{ij}\,n_in_j.
\label{eq:14}
\end{align}

Let us now simplify the last term of \eqref{eq:14}. We again partition the edge set of $G_{2s+1}$ according to the block structure of its adjacency matrix. 
The subgraph of $G_{2s+1}$ induced by the first $s$ vertices is a clique thus
                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                      
\begin{equation*}
    2\sum_{1\le i<j\le s} n_i n_j
    = \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{s} n_i\Bigr)^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{s} n_i^2.
\end{equation*}

Similarly, the subgraph of $G_{2s+1}$ induced by the vertices indexed by $\{s+1,\dots,2s\}$ is a clique and 
\begin{equation*}
    2\sum_{s+1\le i<j\le 2s} n_i n_j
    = \Bigl(\sum_{i=s+1}^{2s} n_i\Bigr)^2 - \sum_{i=s+1}^{2s} n_i^2.
\end{equation*}



The edges between these two halves (the first $s$ and the next $s$ vertices) follow the same pattern as in $G_{2s+1}$. Thus the set of crossing edges is
\begin{equation*}
    E_{\mathrm{cross}}
    = \bigl\{(i,j): 2 \le i \le s,\;\; 2s - i + 2 \le j \le 2s\bigr\},
\end{equation*}
and therefore they contribute
\begin{equation*}
    2\sum_{i=2}^{s} \;\sum_{j=\,2s-i+2}^{\,2s} n_i n_j.
\end{equation*}



Finally, the vertex indexed by $2s+1$ in $G_{2s+1}$, is adjacent to every other vertex. Therefore the edges incident with part $2s+1$ contribute
\begin{equation*}
    2\sum_{i=1}^{2s} n_{2s+1} n_i
    = 2n\,n_{2s+1} - 2n_{2s+1}^2,
\end{equation*}
                                    




Substituting these four contributions into the edge–sum term of~\eqref{eq:14} and then adding the diagonal
contribution
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{2s+1} (n_i - 1)^2
= \sum_{i=1}^{2s+1} (n_i^2 - 2n_i + 1),
\]
we obtain
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{tr}(M^2)
& = \sum_{i=1}^{2s+1} (n_i^2 - 2n_i + 1)+ \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{s} n_i\Bigr)^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{s} n_i^2 + \Bigl(\sum_{i=s+1}^{2s} n_i\Bigr)^2 - \sum_{i=s+1}^{2s} n_i^2  \\
&\quad\quad\hspace{3cm}+ 2\sum_{i=2}^{s}\;\sum_{j=\,2s-i+2}^{\,2s} n_i n_j + 2n\,n_{2s+1} - 2n_{2s+1}^2 \\
&= \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{s} n_i\Bigr)^2
   + \Bigl(\sum_{i=s+1}^{2s} n_i\Bigr)^2
   + 2\sum_{i=2}^{s} \;\sum_{j=\,2s-i+2}^{\,2s} n_i n_j \\
&\quad\quad\hspace{3cm}
   + \sum_{i=1}^{2s+1} (n_i^2 - 2n_i + 1)
   - \sum_{i=1}^{2s} n_i^2
   + 2n\,n_{2s+1} - 2n_{2s+1}^2.
\end{align*}

The square–sum terms simplify to
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{2s+1} n_i^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{2s} n_i^2 - 2n_{2s+1}^2= -\,n_{2s+1}^2,
\]
and 
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{2s+1}(-2n_i + 1) = -2n + 2s+1.
\]
Substituting these back yields exactly
\[
\operatorname{tr}(M^2)
= \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{s} n_i\Bigr)^2
  + \Bigl(\sum_{i=s+1}^{2s} n_i\Bigr)^2
  + 2\sum_{i=2}^{s} \;\sum_{j=\,2s-i+2}^{\,2s} n_i n_j
  \;-\; n_{2s+1}^2
  \;+\; 2n\,n_{2s+1}
  \;+\; (2s+1) - 2n,
\]
This yields the claimed formula.

label: eq:omega-bound
title: Theorem
body_md:
Let \( G = B_4(n_1, n_2, n_3, n_4) \) be a graph of order $n$ with positive integers \( n_1, n_2, n_3, n_4 \). Let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3,\lambda_4$ be  the adjacency eigenvalues of $G$ different from $-1$.                                                   
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:omega-bound}
\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{4}\lambda_i^2}\;\le\; n\!\left(1-\frac{1}{\omega}\right),
\end{equation}
except when
\( (n_1,n_2,n_3,n_4)=(1,1,1,1)
\).

label: eq:trM2-omega
title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:char_polynomial}, the matrix \( M \) has eigenvalues 
\( \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3, \lambda_4 \). In particular,
\[
    \operatorname{tr}(M^2) = \sum_{i=1}^{4} \lambda_i^2.
\] Hence the Wilf-type bound \eqref{eq:omega-bound} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trM2-omega}
    \operatorname{tr}(M^2)\;\le\; n^2\!\left(1-\frac{1}{\omega}\right)^2.
\end{equation}

We set
\[
    p := n_1 + n_2,\quad q := n_3 + n_4,\quad  \omega \geq \max\{p,q\},  \quad n= p + q=\sum_{i=1}^{4}n_i.
\]
To establish \eqref{eq:trM2-omega}, we consider the following three cases:
\[
    \text{(1) } p > q,\qquad \text{(2) } p = q,\qquad \text{(3) } p < q.
\]
                                                                                      
                                      





\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Case 1: $p>q$.}\\
In this case $\omega\geq\max\{p,q\}=p$ and $s=2$. 
                                                          
    
                                       
                                             
                                                                       
              
    
Put $s=2$ in \eqref{eq:13} to obtain \eqref{eq:trM2-omega} with $\omega \ge p$. 
It therefore suffices to prove:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:even-general}
p^2 
+ q^2 
+ 2  n_2n_4 - 2n + 4 
\;\leq\; n^2\!\left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right)^2.
\end{equation}
Expanding the right-hand side,
\[
n^2\!\left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right)^2
= n^2 - \frac{2n^2}{p} + \frac{n^2}{p^2}.
\]
Since
\[
n^2= (p+q)^2
= p^2 
  + q^2 
  + 2 p q,
\]
inequality \eqref{eq:even-general} can be rewritten as
\begin{align*}
p^2 
+ q^2 
+ 2  n_2n_4 - 2n + 4  \leq 
 p^2 
  + q^2 
  + 2 p q  - \frac{2n^2}{p} + \frac{n^2}{p^2}.
\end{align*}


Cancelling the common terms from both sides yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gen-s-ineq}
2n_2n_4 - 2n + 4 \;\le\; 
  2pq - \frac{2n^2}{p} + \frac{n^2}{p^2}.
\end{equation}
Since $n = p+q$, we rewrite \eqref{eq:gen-s-ineq} as
\begin{equation}\label{eq4.2}
2n_2n_4 - 2(p+q) + 4 \;\le\;
  2pq - 2(p+q)\left(1 + \frac{q}{p}\right)
  + \left(1 + \frac{q}{p}\right)^2.
\end{equation}
Rewriting the above inequality, we get the following


\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
    0
    &\leq 
    2pq - 2n_2 n_4 - 2(p+q) \frac{q}{p} + \left(1+ \frac{q}{p}\right)^2-4\\
    &= 2pq - 2n_2n_4 - 2q - 2 \frac{q^2}{p}  +  \frac{q^2}{p^2} + 2 \frac{q}{p}-3,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

                             
                
                  
                                             
                                                    
                                                  
              
                                                  

For the worst case (to minimize the right-hand side) we make the negative term
$-2n_2n_4$ as small as possible. Since
\[
n_2 \le p-1,\qquad n_4 \le q-1,
\]
we have
\[
n_2n_4 \le (p-1)(q-1)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
-2n_2n_4 \;\ge\; -2(p-1)(q-1).
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
    &2pq - 2n_2n_4 - 2q - 2 \frac{q^2}{p}  +  \frac{q^2}{p^2} + 2 \frac{q}{p}-3\\
    &\hspace{3cm}\geq2pq - 2(p-1)(q-1)  - 2q - 2 \frac{q^2}{p}  +  \frac{q^2}{p^2} + 2 \frac{q}{p}-3\\
    &\hspace{3cm}=2pq - 2(pq-p-q+1) - 2q - 2 \frac{q^2}{p}  +  \frac{q^2}{p^2} + 2 \frac{q}{p}-3\\
    &\hspace{3cm}=2p + 2q - 2 - 2q - 2 \frac{q^2}{p}  +  \frac{q^2}{p^2} + 2 \frac{q}{p}-3\\
    &\hspace{3cm}=2p  - 2 \frac{q^2}{p}  +  \frac{q^2}{p^2} + 2 \frac{q}{p}-5.
\end{align*}

                                  
                
              
                    
                        
                        
                                     
                          
               
                         
                          
                        
              
                                
                                  
                          
            
                                                                 
                

Now to complete Case~1 it suffices to show that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Hminus4}
    2p - 2\frac{q^2}{p} + \frac{q^2}{p^2} + 2\frac{q}{p} - 5 \;\ge\; 0.
\end{equation}
for all integers $p\ge3$, $q\ge2$ with $q \le p-1$ and $p>q$.  
               
                                    
                                                                         
                
Since $p>0$, multiplying \eqref{eq:Hminus4} by $p^2$ preserves the inequality and gives
\[
    p^2\!\left(
      2p - 2\frac{q^2}{p} + \frac{q^2}{p^2} + 2\frac{q}{p} - 5
    \right)
    = 2p^3 - 5p^2 + 2pq - 2pq^2 + q^2.
\]
        
    
          
                                           
    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              
                                                                                
                                                
Define, for a fixed $p\geq 3$,
\[
    f_p(q)
    := 2p^3 - 5p^2 + 2pq - 2pq^2 + q^2
     = (1-2p)q^2 + 2pq + (2p^3-5p^2).
\]
Then \eqref{eq:Hminus4} is equivalent to $f_p(q)\ge 0$ for all integers
$2\le q\le p-1$. Note that $f_p(q)$ is a quadratic in $q$ with leading coefficient
$1-2p<0$ (since $p\ge3$), so $f$ opens downward. Then $f(q)$ achieve its maximum at
\[
    q_{\mathrm{v}}
    = -\frac{2p}{2(1-2p)}
    = \frac{p}{2p-1},
\]
and for $p\ge3$ we have $q_{\mathrm{v}} \le \tfrac{3}{5} < 1$.
Hence $f$ is strictly decreasing on $[2,\infty)$.

In our range $2 \le q \le p-1$, the minimum of $f$ is therefore attained at
$q=p-1$. A direct computation yields
\begin{align*}
    f(p-1)
    &=(1-2p)(p-1)^2 + 2p(p-1)+(2p^3 - 5p^2)= 2p^2 - 6p + 1.
\end{align*}
The polynomial $g(p) := 2p^2 - 6p + 1$ is upward-opening, with discriminant $\Delta = 28,$
so its roots are
\[
    p = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{28}}{4}
      = \frac{3 \pm \sqrt{7}}{2}.
\]
Thus $g(p) \ge 0$ for all integers $p \ge 3$. Consequently
$f(q) \ge 0$
for all integers $p \ge 3$ and $2 \le q \le p-1$ and hence \eqref{eq:Hminus4} holds.                                              


                          


\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Case 2: $p=q$.}\\
Here $\omega\geq \max\{p,q\}=p=q$, so $n=2p$ and $q/p=1$. Returning to \eqref{eq4.2} and
substituting $q/p=1$ and $n=2p$, the right-hand side becomes
\[
2pq - 2n\!\left(1+\frac{q}{p}\right) + \left(1+\frac{q}{p}\right)^2
= 2p^2 - 2n\cdot 2 + 2^2
= 2p^2 - 4n + 4
= 2p^2 - 8p + 4.
\]
Thus \eqref{eq4.2} is equivalent to
\begin{align*}
2 n_2n_4 - 2n + 4 \;\le\; 2p^2 - 4n + 4
&\;\Longleftrightarrow\; 2 n_2n_4 \;\le\; 2p^2 - 2n\\
&\;\Longleftrightarrow\; n_2n_4 \;\le\; p^2 - n
 = p(p-2).
\end{align*}

On the other hand, using $n_1+n_2=p$ and $n_3+n_4=q=p$ with $n_i\ge1$ we have
$1\le n_2\le p-1$ and $1\le n_4\le p-1$, so
\[
n_2n_4 \;\le\; (p-1)^2 .
\]
Comparing, we see that the inequality
\[
n_2n_4 \;\le\; p(p-2)
\]
holds  
          
    
                         
    
           
whenever $n_2$ or $n_4$ is at most $p-2$. The only way this inequality 
fails is when 
 $n_2=n_4=p-1$ (consequently $n_1=p-n_2=1$ and $n_3=p-n_4=1$), i.e., when 
\[
(n_1,n_2,n_3,n_4)=(1,p-1,\,1,p-1).
\]
Now we show that \eqref{eq:omega-bound} holds for all \(p\ge3\)
and fails only for \(p=2\), i.e., only for \((n_1,n_2,n_3,n_4)=(1,1,1,1)\).

In this case, the clique number 
\[
\omega\geq 2p-2.
\] 
A direct substitution $n_1=n_3=1 $ and $n_2=n_4=p-1$ into
\eqref{eq:13} gives                                                                                                                                                                            
\[
\operatorname{tr}(M^2)=4p^2-8p+6.
\]
With $n=2p$ and $\omega\ge 2p-2$, we have
\[
n^2\!\left(1-\frac{1}{\omega}\right)^2
\ge (2p)^2\left(1-\frac{1}{2p-2}\right)^2.
\]
Expanding the left-hand side gives
\[
(2p)^2\left(1-\frac{1}{2p-2}\right)^2
=4p^2\cdot \frac{(2p-3)^2}{4(p-1)^2}
=\frac{p^2(2p-3)^2}{(p-1)^2}
=\frac{4p^4-12p^3+9p^2}{(p-1)^2}.
\]
Therefore, to prove \eqref{eq:omega-bound} it suffices to show
\[
4p^2-8p+6 \le \frac{4p^4-12p^3+9p^2}{(p-1)^2},
\]
equivalently it reduce to
\[
0\le (4p^4-12p^3+9p^2)-(4p^2-8p+6)(p-1)^2 
=4p^3-17p^2+20p-6.
\]
Set
\[
f(p):=4p^3-17p^2+20p-6.
\]
Then $f(2)=-2<0$, so the inequality fails at $p=2$, i.e., for $(n_1,n_2,n_3,n_4)=(1,1,1,1)$.
Moreover,
\[
f'(p)=12p^2-34p+20,
\]
whose real roots are \(p=\frac{10}{12}<2\) and \(p=\frac{24}{12}=2\), so
\(f'(p)>0\) for all \(p>2\). Hence \(f(p)\) is strictly increasing on
\((2,\infty)\) and since \(f(3)=9>0\), we obtain \(f(p)>0\) for every
integer \(p\ge3\). Therefore \eqref{eq:omega-bound} holds for all \(p\ge3\)
and fails only at \(p=2\), that is, only for \((n_1,n_2,n_3,n_4)=(1,1,1,1)\). This completes the proof of Case 2. 

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Case 3: $p<q$.}\\
                  
This case is symmetric to Case~1 after interchanging the roles of $p$ and $q$, so the same argument proves \eqref{eq:omega-bound}. This completes the proof.

title: Example
body_md:
Consider the graph $B_4(2,3,1,2)$ in Example~\ref{example1}. The spectrum of $B_4(2,3,1,2)$ is
\[
\{\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3,\lambda_4,-1,-1,-1,-1\},
\]
where
\[
\lambda_1 \approx 5.09,\quad
\lambda_2 \approx 1.63,\quad
\lambda_3 \approx -2.30,\quad
\lambda_4 \approx -0.42.
\]
                                                                                    

Therefore
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{4}\lambda_i^2
\approx (5.09)^2+(1.63)^2+(2.30)^2+(0.42)^2
\approx 34,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{4}\lambda_i^2}\approx 5.83.
\]
Here $n=8$ and $\omega\geq\max\{n_1+n_2,\ n_3+n_4\}=\max\{5,3\}=5$, so
\[
n\!\left(1-\frac{1}{\omega}\right)
\geq8\!\left(1-\frac{1}{5}\right)
=\frac{32}{5}=6.40.
\]
Hence
\[
\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{4}\lambda_i^2}\approx 5.83 \le 6.40 \leq n\!\left(1-\frac{1}{\omega}\right).
\]
